primary_cause: Repricing of mall cash-flow risk and rent nonpayment risk. The live overhang remained SPG's earlier closure of all U.S. malls due to COVID-19
secondary_factors: IMF Great Lockdown recession framing and renewed focus on earnings-season damage to consumer-facing real estate
store_description: SPG's April 13 decline looks most consistent with investors revisiting the implications of a full mall shutdown after Simon had already closed all domestic properties on March 18. The IMF projecting global GDP down 3% in 2020 deepened the expected rent and occupancy hit.

primary_cause: Ongoing repricing of away-from-home demand destruction. Coca-Cola warned on March 20 that it did not expect to achieve prior 2020 guidance reflecting heavy exposure to restaurants theaters and other away-from-home channels
secondary_factors: Rotation out of defensives as investors shifted attention to earnings season and recession forecasts
store_description: KO's drop was likely driven by the market continuing to absorb the implication of its prior guidance withdrawal. A large slice of volume was tied to shut venues making a 2020 miss of prior targets increasingly unavoidable.

primary_cause: Anticipation of severe Q1 reserve builds and credit losses ahead of earnings. Investors bracing for very large reserve builds and weak revenue quality
secondary_factors: Broader recession fears and concerns around dividend/capital actions for banks
store_description: WFC's April 13 selloff was primarily an earnings-preview move. That concern was validated the next day when Wells reported a $3.1 billion reserve build and $950 million of securities impairment with first-quarter results hit materially by COVID-related charges.

primary_cause: Anticipation of very large loan-loss provisioning in Q1 results due the next day
secondary_factors: IMF recession fears and mounting U.S. fiscal deterioration estimates
store_description: JPM's April 13 decline was an earnings-risk move that proved justified one day later when JPMorgan reported Q1 net income of $2.9 billion with credit costs of $8.3 billion including $6.8 billion of reserve builds.

primary_cause: Anticipation of heavy reserve building and profit compression into earnings. Market was discounting large credit provisioning across the big-bank group
secondary_factors: Recession fears and concern about consumer/corporate loan quality
store_description: BAC's drop looks like pre-earnings credit-risk repricing. The next session validated that view when Reuters reported BAC profit fell and it had built a $3.6 billion reserve buffer with total provisions more than 3x actual first-quarter loan losses.

primary_cause: Continuing repricing of liquidity stress and shutdown-driven demand collapse. The active overhang remained GM's March 24 move to draw about $16 billion from credit lines and suspend 2020 guidance
secondary_factors: Deepening recession forecasts and uncertainty on U.S. auto-plant restart timing
store_description: GM's April 13 weakness was most likely a continuation of the market's negative view on automakers with shuttered production and emergency liquidity moves. Drawing $16 billion to beef up liquidity had already signaled how severe the cash-flow shock could become.

primary_cause: Sector-style repricing of utilities under recession and demand-risk assumptions rather than a fresh Duke-specific headline
secondary_factors: Falling commercial/industrial demand expectations and defensive-sector rotation
store_description: No evidence of a discrete Duke event causing the April 13 drop. This looks more like utilities being marked down on fears of weaker usage mix and a worsening macro outlook even though Duke indicated its systems remained staffed and operating.

primary_cause: Anticipation of COVID-related demand destruction in equipment markets. Later reporting confirmed Deere's quarterly profit fell 41% as equipment demand weakened
secondary_factors: General industrial cyclicals weakness amid IMF recession forecasts
store_description: Deere's move appears to have been a forward-looking cyclical selloff rather than a response to a single headline. Investors were likely pricing in demand damage that later showed up in results including large declines in farm turf construction and forestry equipment sales.

primary_cause: Anticipation of outsized consumer-credit losses and reserve builds. As a consumer-credit-heavy lender COF was especially exposed to the reserve-build theme heading into earnings season
secondary_factors: Recession fears and concern over unemployment-driven card/auto defaults
store_description: COF likely fell more than diversified banks because its credit-card and consumer-loan exposure made the COVID shock look particularly dangerous. That concern was later borne out by a $5.4 billion credit-loss provision and a quarterly net loss.

primary_cause: Anticipation that market volatility and the March selloff would hit AUM-sensitive earnings. No negative BLK-specific release on April 10-12
secondary_factors: Broad pressure on asset managers from recession fears and risk-off positioning ahead of results
store_description: BLK's drop appears to have been an earnings-positioning move ahead of a quarter expected to show pressure from March's market dislocation. BlackRock later reported profit down 23% to $806 million while AUM slipped to $6.47 trillion validating the caution.

primary_cause: Pre-earnings financial-sector de-risking. No new BK-specific announcement and BNY Mellon was scheduled to report on April 16
secondary_factors: Concern that lower rates and market stress would hurt net interest revenue and fee visibility
store_description: BK's move looks like sympathy with the broader bank/financial complex ahead of ugly Q1 reports. BNY's actual Q1 report later showed net income down 32% sequentially to $944 million and a $169 million provision for credit losses.

primary_cause: Anticipation of collapse in billed business travel spend and rising card credit losses. AXP later disclosed it had suspended share repurchases in March
secondary_factors: Broader bank/consumer-credit earnings fears
store_description: AXP traded like one of the most COVID-exposed financials because its business was tied to travel entertainment and affluent card spending. The market's concern about capital preservation was real as the company later confirmed it had suspended share repurchases in mid-March.

primary_cause: Likely macro/sector repricing of REITs rather than a company-specific catalyst in the window
secondary_factors: General earnings-season risk and recession fears
store_description: Cannot support a stock-specific primary catalyst from the prior 3 days with confidence. This looks more like a REIT basket move in a market still reassessing funding costs tenant risk and recession severity.

primary_cause: Anticipation of client spending slowdowns in consulting/IT services. No fresh Accenture-specific negative release in the window
secondary_factors: Broader earnings-season derisking
store_description: ACN's decline appears tied to expectations that clients would slash discretionary consulting budgets as COVID uncertainty deepened. No precise company headline was found so this is a fundamentals-based de-rating rather than news reaction.

primary_cause: Repricing of industrial and aerospace exposure into a deeper recession. No fresh HON-specific negative headline in the window
secondary_factors: General cyclicals weakness and pandemic factory disruptions
store_description: HON's move was likely driven by deteriorating end-market expectations especially aerospace and industrial demand rather than a fresh company statement. The absence of a weekend catalyst lowers confidence.

primary_cause: Bad Q1 earnings and large reserve build. On April 14 Wells reported a $3.1 billion reserve build and $950 million of securities impairment with a major COVID-related earnings hit
secondary_factors: Investor worry about future credit losses and capital actions
store_description: This one is straightforward. Wells results confirmed severe pandemic stress with large reserve additions and impairment charges that swamped profitability so the 4.0% decline was directly earnings-driven.

primary_cause: Continued repricing of Boeing's liquidity and demand crisis not a new April 11-13 headline. Main active issues were ongoing MAX grounding/cash burn and severe COVID-driven aviation demand destruction
secondary_factors: Broad industrial/aerospace recession fears
store_description: Boeing's April 14 decline looks like continuation of the same solvency-and-recovery trade that dominated the stock in spring 2020 with the MAX still grounded and commercial aviation crushed by the pandemic.

primary_cause: Small-business stress and weak macro data hurting expectations for QuickBooks/small-business ecosystem demand. No clear Intuit-specific corporate release in the April 12-14 window
secondary_factors: Broad software multiple compression on a weak tape
store_description: Cannot point to a company-specific INTU headline in the prior 3 days. The best-supported explanation is investors marked down names exposed to small-business formation payroll and accounting activity as the economy deteriorated.

primary_cause: Post-earnings negative read-through from huge reserve builds and weak outlook. JPM had reported the day before with a 68% profit slump and $8.3 billion of credit costs
secondary_factors: IMF Great Lockdown recession narrative and ugly U.S. economic data
store_description: JPM's second leg down on April 15 was not random. The market focused on how severe and potentially persistent the reserve cycle could be especially after analysts said the provisions were greater than expected and might continue into Q2.

primary_cause: Macro-driven industrial demand fears rather than a verified company-specific headline. No Linde-specific negative announcement in the April 12-14 window
secondary_factors: IMF recession outlook and cyclicals selloff
store_description: For LIN the evidence points more to a cyclical macro re-rating than to company news. Industrial gases names were exposed to the same sharp contraction fears that hit global manufacturing-sensitive stocks as the IMF projected minus 3.0% world growth for 2020.
